paragraphs: “He talks very coherently,” thought Ivan, “even if he does mumble. So what’s this derangement of his faculties that Herzenstube talked about?”
“You’re being cunning with me, damn you!” he exclaimed, getting angry.
“But I thought at the time that you had guessed perfectly well, sir,” Smerdyakov parried with the simplest air.
“If I’d guessed, I’d have stayed,” cried Ivan.
“Why, I thought it was because you’d guessed that you went away in such a hurry, only to get out of trouble, only to run away and save yourself in your fright.”
“You think everyone is as great a coward as you are?”
“Forgive me, I thought you were like me.”

“Of course, I ought to have guessed,” Ivan said in agitation, “and I did guess there was some mischief brewing on your part ... only you’re lying, you’re lying again,” he cried, suddenly remembering. “Do you remember how you came up to the carriage and said to me, ‘It’s always worth while speaking to a clever man’? So you were glad I was going away, since you praised me?”
Smerdyakov sighed again and again. A trace of color came into his face.

“If I was pleased,” he said, rather breathlessly, “it was simply because you agreed to go not to Moscow but to Tchermashnya. For it was nearer, anyway. Only when I said those words to you, it was not by way of praise but of reproach. You didn’t understand it.”
“What reproach?”
“Why, that foreseeing such a calamity you deserted your own father and would not protect us. For I might have been taken up at any time for stealing that three thousand.”
“Damn you!” Ivan swore again. “Wait, did you tell the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer about those knocks?”
“I told them everything just as it was.”
Ivan was inwardly amazed again.

“If I thought of anything then,” he began again, “it was only of some wickedness on your part. Dmitri might kill him, but that he would steal—I didn’t believe that then.... But I was ready for any wickedness from you. You told me yourself you could sham a fit. What did you say that for?”

“It was just my simplicity, sir, and I’ve never shammed a fit on purpose in my life. And I only said so then to boast to you. It was just foolishness. I liked you so much then, and was open-hearted with you.”
“My brother accuses you outright of the murder and the theft.”

“What else is left for him to do?” said Smerdyakov with a bitter grin. “And who will believe him, with all the proofs against him? Grigory Vassilyevitch saw the door open. What can he say after that? But never mind him! He’s trembling to save himself.”
He slowly stopped speaking; then suddenly, as though on reflection, he added:

“And look here again. He wants to throw it on me and make out it’s the work of my hands—I’ve heard that already. But as to my being clever at shamming a fit: would I have told you beforehand that I could sham one, if I really had had such a design against your father? If I had been planning such a murder, could I have been such a fool as to give such evidence against myself beforehand? And to his son, too! I swear! Is that likely? As if that could be—such a thing has never happened. No one hears this talk of ours now except Providence itself, and if you were to tell it to the prosecutor and Nikolay Parfenovitch you might defend me completely by doing so. For who would be likely to be such a criminal, if he is so open-hearted beforehand? Anyone can see that.”

“Well,” said Ivan, and he got up to cut the conversation short, struck by Smerdyakov’s last argument, “I don’t suspect you at all, and I think it’s absurd, in fact, to suspect you. On the contrary, I’m grateful to you for setting my mind at rest. Now I’m going, but I’ll come again. Meanwhile, good-by. Get well. Is there anything you want?”
“I’m very thankful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn’t forget me, and provides me with anything I want, out of her kindness. Good people visit me every day.”
“Good-by. But I won’t say anything about your being able to sham a fit, and I don’t advise you to, either,” something made Ivan say suddenly.
“I quite understand, sir. And if you don’t speak of that, I shall say nothing of that conversation of ours at the gate.”

So Ivan went out, and only when he had gone a dozen steps along the corridor did he suddenly feel that there was an insulting meaning in Smerdyakov’s last words. He almost turned back, but it was only a passing impulse. Muttering “Nonsense!” he left the hospital.

His chief feeling was one of relief that it was Mitya, not Smerdyakov, who had committed the murder, though one might have expected the opposite. He did not want to analyze the reason for this feeling, and even felt a real aversion to prying into his own sensations. He felt as if he wanted to hurry up and forget something. In the following days he became convinced of Mitya’s guilt as he learned the full weight of the evidence against him. There was testimony from people of no importance, Fenya and her mother, for instance, but its effect was almost overwhelming. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern, and at Plotnikov’s shop, as well as the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence seemed conclusive. It was the details that were so damning. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers almost as much as Grigory’s evidence about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa, in answer to Ivan’s questions, declared that Smerdyakov had been lying all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed.” Although she was a sound sleeper, she had woken several times and heard him moaning. “He was moaning the whole time, moaning continually.”
When Ivan talked to Herzenstube and gave his opinion that Smerdyakov was not mad but only rather weak, all he got from the old man was a subtle smile.

“Do you know how he spends his time now?” he asked. “Learning lists of French words by heart. He has an exercise book under his pillow with the French words written out in Russian letters for him by somebody, he he he!”

Ivan ended by dismissing all doubts. He could not think of Dmitri without revulsion. Only one thing was strange, however. Alyosha persisted that Dmitri was not the murderer and that “in all probability” Smerdyakov was. Ivan always felt that Alyosha’s opinion meant a great deal to him, so he was astonished at it now. Another strange thing was that Alyosha made no attempt to talk about Mitya with Ivan, never began on the subject and only answered his questions. This, too, struck Ivan particularly.

But at that time he was very much preoccupied with something quite apart from all that. On his return from Moscow, he had abandoned himself hopelessly to his mad and consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This is not the time to begin speaking of that new passion of Ivan’s, which left its mark on all the rest of his life. It would furnish the subject for another novel, which I may perhaps never write. But I cannot omit to mention here that when Ivan, on leaving Katerina Ivanovna with Alyosha, as I’ve related already, told him, “I am not keen on her,” it was an absolute lie. He loved her madly, though at times he hated her so much that he might have murdered her. Many causes helped to bring about this feeling. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, she had rushed to meet Ivan on his return as her one salvation. She was hurt, insulted and humiliated in her feelings. And now there had come back to her the man who had loved her so ardently before (oh! she knew that very well), and whose heart and intellect she considered far superior to her own. But the sternly virtuous girl did not give herself up altogether to the man she loved, in spite of the Karamazov violence of his passions and the great fascination he had for her. At the same time she was continually tormented by remorse for having deserted Mitya, and in moments of discord and violent anger (and there were many) she told Ivan so plainly. This was what he had called, to Alyosha, “lies upon lies.” There was, of course, much that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything.... But of all this later.

He did, in fact, almost forget Smerdyakov’s existence for a time, and yet, two weeks after his first visit to him, he began to be haunted by the same strange thoughts as before. It’s enough to say that he kept asking himself why, on that last night in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, he had crept out onto the stairs like a thief and listened to hear what his father was doing below. Why had he recalled that afterwards with repulsion? Why, the next morning, had he suddenly been so depressed on the journey? Why, as he reached Moscow, had he said to himself, “I am a scoundrel”? And now he almost imagined that these tormenting thoughts would make him forget even Katerina Ivanovna, so completely did they take possession of him again. It was just after imagining this that he met Alyosha in the street. He stopped him at once and put a question to him:

“Do you remember when Dmitri burst in after dinner and beat father, and afterwards I told you in the yard that I reserved ‘the right to desire’?... Tell me, did you think then that I desired father’s death or not?”
“I did think so,” answered Alyosha softly.

“It was so, too. It wasn’t a matter of guessing. But didn’t you imagine then that what I wished was just that ‘one reptile should devour another’; that is, just that Dmitri should kill father, and as soon as possible ... and that I myself was even prepared to help bring that about?”
Alyosha turned rather pale and looked silently into his brother’s face.
“Speak!” cried Ivan. “I want above everything to know what you thought then. I want the truth, the truth!”
He drew a deep breath, looking angrily at Alyosha before the answer came.
“Forgive me, I did think that, too, at the time,” whispered Alyosha, and he did not add one softening phrase.

“Thanks,” snapped Ivan, and leaving Alyosha, he went quickly on his way. From that time Alyosha noticed that Ivan began obviously to avoid him and even seemed to have taken a dislike to him, so much so that Alyosha gave up going to see him. Right after that meeting with Alyosha, Ivan did not go home but went straight to Smerdyakov again.
